title: NDA clauses to flag - scratchpad
content:
Purpose: quick personal checklist for NDA redlines and on-call negotiation bullets. Not canonical; bits I want handy during syncs/calls.

Context notes:
- For partner pilot deals, we want narrow use + limited re-use/aggregate rights.
- For platform integrations, watch for broad data rights and audit burdens.
- Customer asks for ability to store/retain models or outputs — say no / require narrow license.

Top clauses to watch (fast reference):

1) Definition of Confidential Information
- Why matter: defines what we must protect; overly broad = everything is confidential.
- Redline approach: carve out general knowledge, residuals, independently developed, public domain.
- Suggested language snippet: "Confidential Information excludes information that (a) is or becomes public other than by Recipient's breach; (b) was known to Recipient without restriction prior to disclosure; (c) is independently developed by Recipient without use of Discloser’s Confidential Information; (d) is received from a third party without restriction."
- Talking point: we can’t operate if they claim every remark or bug report is confidential. Ask for examples.

2) Use limitation / permitted purpose
- Why matter: controls how partner can use our data/outputs.
- Redline approach: define narrow permitted purpose (e.g., evaluation/integration/pilot) and forbid training or model improvement without explicit license.
- Counter: "Recipient may use Confidential Information solely to perform the integration and improve the mutual integration; Recipient shall not use Confidential Information to train models or improve models without prior written consent."
- Talking point: model training rights have long-term value — keep them out of standard NDAs.

3) Data retention & deletion
- Why: long tails + liability.
- Redline: retention limits, deletion on termination + certification of deletion, exception for backups with timeline.
- Snippet: "Recipient will delete or irreversibly anonymize Discloser’s Customer Data within 30 days of termination, except for backups which will be destroyed within 90 days."
- Ask: what logging/backups do they have? need SOC evidence.

4) Aggregation / derivative use / anonymized data
- Why: partners often want to use aggregated data for analytics — ok if truly de-identified and not re-identifying; but watch for rights to build models.
- Redline: permit aggregate analytics that do not identify Discloser and prohibit model training unless agreed.

5) IP ownership / outputs & inventions
- Why: who owns product of collaboration? model outputs? code?
- Redline approach: Background IP stays with owner; deliverables under SOW can be assigned or licensed; outputs of models remain with the customer only if explicitly stated.
- Example ask: "All background materials remain the respective party’s property. Any deliverables defined in a Statement of Work shall be owned as set forth in that SOW. No party acquires rights to the other’s algorithms or models."

6) Residuals clause (developer-friendly language)
- Why: cannot prevent someone from using know-how retained in memory.
- Redline: residuals allowed in limited way. Avoid language that prevents use of general skills or residuals.
- Quick line: "Recipient may use general knowledge retained in unaided memory without obligation."

7) Indemnity and liability cap
- Why: catastrophic exposure risk.
- Redline approach: push for mutual indemnities, carve out indirect / consequential damages, liability cap equal to fees paid in prior 12 months or a fixed cap. Exclude breaches of confidentiality and willful misconduct from cap? discuss.
- Talking strategy: we accept carve-outs for IP infringement; avoid broad 3rd-party claims that drag us in.

8) Confidentiality duration
- Why: how long do obligations last? perpetual for trade secrets, 2–5 years for others.
- Redline: 3 years for general CI, perpetual for trade secrets.

9) Audit rights and on-site inspections
- Why: customers sometimes want audits — operationally expensive and risky.
- Redline: limited audit rights, remote-only, notice period, scope-limited to SOC-equivalent evidence. Prefer certified reports instead.

10) Subprocessors / subcontracting / transfer
- Why: who else sees data? cloud providers, subsidiaries.
- Redline: require notice and right to object to new subprocessors, ensure flow-down obligations and security standards.
- Ask: list of subprocessors upfront.

11) Security standards & breach notification
- Why: SLA on notification timing and contents.
- Redline: notify within 72 hours of discovery (or as law requires), share remediation plan, cooperate. Reference ISO/IEC 27001, SOC2 or equivalent.

12) Publicity / press releases
- Why: we don’t want surprise co-marketing or logos.
- Redline: require prior written consent for public use of name/logo/case study.

13) Assignment & change of control
- Why: ensure we aren’t forced into relationship with unknown acquirer.
- Redline: require consent for assignment except to affiliates or as part of sale of business; buyer must assume obligations.

14) Governing law & venue / injunctive relief
- Why: affects enforcement. For Redwood we prefer CA law or neutral; consider injunctive carve for trade secrets.
- Talking point: ask for mediation first for commercial disputes. Keep injunctive for IP.

15) Export controls / sanctions
- Why: compliance risk — need reps/warranties.
- Redline: mutual warranty of compliance with export laws, right to suspend service if sanctions.

Quick negotiation playbook (prep before call):
- Have target language snippets ready for top 5 items: use, retention, liability cap, IP, subprocessors.
- Prioritize: 1) data use/training rights, 2) liability cap/indemnity, 3) retention/deletion, 4) subprocessors, 5) audit.
- Concessions we can give: longer retention for limited pilot, aggregated analytics (with strict de-id), right to publish joint case study with approval.
- Redlines we rarely accept: unlimited indemnity, open-ended training or resale rights, perpetual data retention, forced on-site audits.

Negotiation lines — short scripts: 
- If asked for training rights: "We’re not assigning rights to train or monetize models from your data under this NDA. If you need training rights we should discuss a separate license with pricing."
- If they want broad retention: "We need retention limits and certified deletion post-project; logging/backups OK but with defined windows."
- If they ask for unlimited IP assignment: "Background IP stays with the owner — we can assign specific deliverables in an SOW."

Operational checklist (pre-redline handoff to legal):
- Gather sample data flows, list of subprocessors, compliance reports (SOC2), exact scope of pilot, expected retention windows, any regulatory constraints (HIPAA, PCI, etc.).
- Attach SOW draft if deliverables expected.
- Decide on liability cap floor we can accept (e.g., $250k or 12 months fees).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Do we have precedent NDA for pilot customers with training carve-out? (ask contracts team)
- What’s our default liability cap we can commit to for early-stage partners?
- Confirm list of approved subprocessors and how to present to customers.

Random personal notes / brain-dump: 
- Keep examples at hand: two past deals where training rights were asked and we pushed back hard — helps with tone.
- Prepare a short one-pager for Sales: "What we will not give in standard NDAs".
- Follow-up: sync with Contracts next week; bring SOW template.

End of scratchpad.
